paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost every adult in a wealthy country now carries some proof of loyalty: a plastic card for the supermarket, an app for the coffee chain, a membership number for the airline. The official explanation for these schemes is simple. Customers are rewarded for coming back, and so they come back more often. It is a story that suits both sides, since shoppers enjoy the feeling of getting something for nothing and companies enjoy an image of generosity. I want to suggest that it is largely wrong. Most loyalty schemes do remarkably little to create loyalty. What they actually purchase, and what explains their extraordinary spread, is something rather different.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea is not new. In the 1950s and 1960s, millions of British and American households collected trading stamps, which retailers handed out with purchases and which could be stuck into books and exchanged for kettles, lawnmowers and toys. The stamps faded in the 1970s, a decline that the economic historian Martin Osei attributes mainly to rising inflation, which made shoppers more interested in low prices today than in distant rewards. The modern era began in 1981, when an American airline launched the first large frequent-flyer programme. Within a few years almost every major carrier had copied it, and supermarkets, hotel chains and retailers of every kind soon followed.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If the schemes were truly building loyalty, members should spend more after joining than similar shoppers who do not join. The evidence for this is weak. Helen Marwick, an economist at the University of Castleford, compared the spending of 20,000 supermarket shoppers before and after they signed up to a scheme with that of non-members living in the same areas. She found that the people who joined were overwhelmingly those who already did most of their shopping in that chain, and that their spending barely changed afterwards. In other words, the rewards went largely to customers who would have returned regardless. Taken at face value, this looks like money thrown away.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Why, then, do businesses persist? One answer, offered by the economist Tomas Lindgren, is that schemes survive because of competition rather than in spite of it. Once a rival has a scheme, a firm without one risks losing its most price-conscious customers, so each company keeps its programme not because it pays but because abandoning it alone would cost even more. The result is that every firm bears the expense and none gains a lasting advantage. I find this account persuasive as far as it goes. It explains why schemes are so hard to abolish, but not why companies remain so eager to launch new ones.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The more convincing explanation lies in what members hand over at the till. Every time a card is scanned, the company learns who bought what, when, and at what price. This information allows offers to be tailored to individuals, and its commercial value can be considerable: in a two-year trial run by the Brightwater Consumer Panel, households that received vouchers matched to their own buying habits increased their spending by around four per cent, while those receiving general discounts showed no change. Priya Nair, who studies pricing at Dunmore Business School, goes further. She argues that loyalty data makes possible a quiet form of price discrimination, allowing firms to offer discounts only to customers likely to shop elsewhere while charging everyone else the full price.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Airlines have taken this logic furthest. Their largest source of loyalty income is not passengers but banks, which buy miles in bulk to award to holders of their credit cards. Since many miles are never spent – a phenomenon the industry calls 'breakage' – every point that expires unused is almost pure profit. These programmes have become so lucrative that, during the pandemic, several American carriers raised billions of dollars by pledging them as security for loans, and some analysts valued the schemes above the airlines that ran them. Points, in effect, have become a private currency, issued by companies with no central bank to restrain them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that loyalty schemes are a fraud, or that they should be outlawed. Many members receive genuine savings, and the exchange of data for discounts is one that plenty of people make knowingly. But the word 'loyalty' disguises the nature of the bargain. Members pay, in part, with information about their lives, and those who do not join may pay with higher shelf prices. Regulators should require schemes to state plainly what data they collect and how it is used, so that shoppers can judge for themselves whether the reward is worth the price.
